Authentication flow

Source: vignettes/authentication-flow.Rmd
authentication-flow.Rmd

Overview

shinyOAuth runs the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow inside a Shiny app. The browser visits the provider for login and consent, then returns with an authorization code. shinyOAuth exchanges that code for tokens, validates the response, and updates the module’s reactive authentication state.

The provider object describes the service, the client object holds the app’s registration and policy, and oauth_module_server() manages each Shiny session. The UI wrapper handles the HTTP callback and browser setup. With OpenID Connect (OIDC), the flow also validates identity through a signed ID token. OAuth-only providers such as GitHub and Spotify supply profile information through their own APIs.

The usage vignette contains the application setup. The sequence below describes the work performed by the package after that setup.

Starting login and binding it to the browser

With auto_redirect = TRUE, the module starts login for an unauthenticated session. With auto_redirect = FALSE, auth[["request_login"]]() initiates the same flow. Both paths wait for browser setup before preparing the request.

For each login transaction, the module establishes a fresh random browser binding. The browser holds the binding token in origin- and tab-scoped session storage, with a separate temporary cookie marker. On return, the module checks this binding against the pending transaction. This connects the callback to the browser tab that started it, rather than accepting state from any browser presenting the same callback URL.

The binding is separate from provider-issued access and ID tokens. Browser storage and cookie setup happen through the UI dependency; unavailable browser facilities produce a browser-setup error before login proceeds.

Preparing the authorization request

The authorization builder, also exposed through prepare_call() and prepare_authorization_request(), combines the provider’s authorization endpoint with the client’s ID, redirect URI, scopes and configured request parameters. The module prepares the transaction values used during later validation:

Value How the package uses it
state Carries authenticated, encrypted transaction data and links the callback to the pending login record.
PKCE verifier and challenge The request carries the challenge; the later token exchange supplies the verifier, binding the exchange to this request.
OIDC nonce The returned ID token is checked against the stored nonce when nonce validation is enabled.

Generic OIDC helpers enable PKCE and nonce checks by default. Named provider helpers select defaults appropriate to their service. S256 is the default PKCE method when PKCE is enabled.

Pending state and expiry

The client state store retains the browser binding, PKCE verifier, nonce and transaction context needed for the return. The encrypted state and stored context also record the client/provider policy used to start login. A callback cannot continue under a changed validation policy.

state_payload_max_age limits the encrypted state’s age, while the store’s retention determines how long the pending record remains available. Both default to five minutes. State consumption is single-use, so replaying a completed callback cannot exchange the code again.

The default store belongs to one R process. A shared store and state_key let another process continue the same transaction, with atomic record consumption providing the single-use guarantee across processes.

Authorization at the provider

The module sends the browser to the prepared authorization URL, or submits a browser form when the client selects POST authorization. The provider handles credentials and consent. Existing provider sessions or earlier consent may allow it to return without showing another prompt.

The authorization result contains a short-lived code or an error such as access_denied, together with the transaction state. The provider sends this result to the registered redirect URI. The code is exchanged by R; it is not the access token used in later API calls.

Receiving and validating the callback

oauth_ui() processes query callbacks before application HTML or scripts load. It validates the callback address and response envelope, stores a sealed, short-lived response, and redirects to a clean continuation URL carrying a one-time handle. oauth_form_post_ui() provides the corresponding path for POST callbacks. The wrappers also set no-store and no-referrer response headers.

The HTTP continuation separates callback data from application rendering. It does not complete login by itself: the Shiny module still checks the initiating browser and consumes the pending transaction before code exchange.

Transaction checks

The module checks that the state is authentic and within its lifetime, that the stored client/provider policy still matches, and that the browser binding agrees with the pending record. The callback route and any required issuer identifier are checked against trusted client configuration. Missing, expired, already-consumed or mismatched records reject the callback.

A provider error response goes through state and browser validation too. Only a valid response for this transaction can become the session’s login error.

Several authorization servers

For a configured client registry, the HTTP wrapper selects the client by its registered callback route or issuer. Distinct-route mode checks the callback address. Issuer mode uses the RFC 9207 iss or the JARM response’s issuer as a routing hint; the selected client’s issuer, signature, transaction and browser checks establish trust. The registry does not treat an incoming issuer string as a new trusted provider.

Exchanging the code for tokens

After callback validation, shinyOAuth sends the code to the token endpoint, along with the PKCE verifier and the authentication required by the app’s registration. token_auth_style selects that authentication, such as a client secret, signed assertion or client certificate.

The token response is still untrusted at this point. shinyOAuth parses it, validates the access token and token type, calculates expiry, and reconciles reported scopes with the requested permissions. scope_validation determines whether a reduced grant produces a warning or rejects login. The token records granted_scopes and whether the response explicitly verified that grant in granted_scopes_verified.

For ordinary OAuth responses that omit expires_in, the package uses shinyOAuth.default_expires_in, defaulting to 3,600 seconds. SMART clients apply their separate lifetime policy.

Code exchange and refresh are not automatically retried after ordinary network or HTTP failures, because the provider may already have consumed the code or rotated a refresh credential. DPoP nonce challenges have their own one-retry handling.

Validating identity and profile information

ID token checks

With OIDC validation enabled, shinyOAuth verifies the ID token using the provider’s public signing keys. Key retrieval and caching follow the provider’s configured issuer and JWKS policy. Decoding claims is followed by signature and claim validation before the identity is accepted.

Check What it establishes
Signature and allowed algorithm The token was signed with an acceptable provider key.
iss The token came from the configured issuer.
aud and, when present, azp The token is intended for this client; additional audiences require explicit trust.
sub The token identifies a subject within that issuer.
exp, iat and optional nbf The token is within its validity window.
Nonce, when enabled The ID token belongs to this login request.
auth_time, when freshness was requested The provider login satisfies the requested maximum age.
at_hash, when present or required The ID token agrees with the returned access token.

Time checks allow the configured clock leeway, defaulting to 30 seconds. The package also applies its configured maximum ID-token lifetime, defaulting to 24 hours. Requested claim requirements follow claims_validation, while required_acr_values checks the validated authentication-context claim against the client’s accepted values.

Introspection and UserInfo

With introspect = TRUE, shinyOAuth asks the provider whether the access token is active. The response must report active = TRUE and satisfy the configured introspection_checks. Introspection runs before profile retrieval, allowing it to supply binding information for opaque certificate- or DPoP-bound tokens. Checks involving the profile finish after that profile becomes available.

When userinfo_required = TRUE, the package fetches the provider’s UserInfo endpoint or profile API. A failed required fetch rejects login. For OIDC, when both a validated ID token and UserInfo are available, their sub values must match. The provider’s subject-binding policy can also require a validated ID token to be present for the profile fetch.

UserInfo can be JSON or a signed JWT. Signed responses go through signature and claim validation, and userinfo_signed_jwt_required rejects ordinary JSON when the registration requires signing. OAuth-only helpers obtain their profiles through the service’s API without creating an OIDC identity assertion.

Publishing authentication state

After all configured checks pass, the module publishes the OAuthToken as auth[["token"]] and sets auth[["authenticated"]] to TRUE. Reactive consumers then see the accepted token and available profile. A rejected login instead populates auth[["error"]] and auth[["error_description"]].

The token holds the access and refresh credentials, expiry, granted scopes, validated ID token claims and fetched profile. Additional response parameters are available in extra_fields; initial_extra_fields preserves the initial code-exchange values across refreshes.

The module’s connection() method resolves the current credentials through an OAuthConnection. Connection methods apply session ownership, current access and configured permission checks when obtaining tokens or making requests.

Asynchronous execution

With async = TRUE and mirai workers or a non-sequential future plan, the module dispatches network work to background R processes. The validation sequence is the same, while the main process can continue servicing Shiny. Authentication state is updated after the worker result passes validation. The module checks that a result still belongs to the current authorization, so work completing after logout or replacement cannot restore the old login.

State-store access and hosted Request Object publication remain in the main process. Signed-request preparation, PAR and query-JARM verification can run in workers. Setup-time discovery and POST-wrapper JARM verification remain synchronous. This describes the module’s work; API calls made by application code have their own execution context.

Refresh, reauthentication and logout

Token refresh

The module watches token expiry. With refresh_proactively = TRUE and an available refresh token, it schedules refresh before expiry. Connection token acquisition can also trigger refresh on demand. Overlapping asynchronous refreshes coordinate use of the same credential.

A refresh response passes token validation, configured introspection and any required profile fetch before replacing the current token. A rotated refresh token replaces the previous one. If the provider omits a new ID token, the stored identity token remains; a new ID token is checked for continuity with the original subject, issuer and audience, plus nonce and authentication time when applicable. Certificate-bound tokens require fresh binding data.

Ordinary refresh requests preserve the retained scope limit. SMART clients and API-specific token targets apply their corresponding scope rules. Refresh updates credentials without establishing a new interactive login.

Expiry and maximum login age

By default, token expiry or refresh failure clears the local token and makes authenticated false. An in-progress refresh has a grace period before expiry clearing. reauth_after_seconds independently limits the age of the interactive login; refresh does not restart that timer. With automatic redirects enabled, the module starts authorization again when appropriate.

For OIDC age-based reauthentication, the request includes max_age = 0 and the returned auth_time is checked. OAuth-only providers receive an ordinary new authorization request, which may reuse their existing login session.

indefinite_session = TRUE changes local clearing behavior: the module retains login state after expiry or refresh failure, reports token_stale, and ignores the maximum-login-age limit. This does not extend token validity at the provider. With token targets, individual API tokens can expire while the shared local authorization remains; connection methods check the selected target before use.

Logout and revocation

auth[["logout"]]() clears local credentials and resets the browser binding. It also attempts token revocation when the provider supports it. With revoke_on_session_end = TRUE, session termination and automatic clearing also attempt revocation. These requests follow the module’s sync or async mode; remote failure does not prevent local cleanup.

Provider account sessions are separate, so local logout can be followed by another authorization without a provider password prompt. Retained connections have their own lifetime and ownership rules, described in Multiple authorizations.

Optional protocol extensions

Configured extensions fit into the same sequence rather than requiring a separate application-managed flow:

Extension Package behavior
JAR Signs the authorization parameters as a Request Object before browser navigation. Optional encryption hides the contents.
PAR Sends the request directly to the provider first, then redirects the browser with the returned reference.
Form Post Receives the authorization result by POST and bridges it into the Shiny session.
JARM Verifies the signed authorization response before processing its callback fields; configured encryption adds decryption first.
mTLS Presents the client certificate and uses configured endpoint aliases; certificate-bound token checks apply when enabled.
DPoP Signs proofs and handles nonce challenges for token requests and resource requests made through the configured connection or request helpers.

Advanced security describes these configurations. Detailed contracts are documented under oauth_client(), oauth_provider(), handle_callback() and refresh_token().

Audit trail

The flow emits events for request preparation, callback checks, token operations and authentication-state changes. Related events share a trace_id, and failed checks include operation or phase context. The configured audit hook receives these events; OpenTelemetry can export the same events and operation timings. The audit logging and OpenTelemetry vignettes describe those records.
